name: The adversaries of Judah and Benjamin
charge: Weakening the hands of the people; hiring counsellors against them to frustrate the building of the house of God
summary: The people of the land offered to help build the temple and were refused, and turned to hindrance: hired counsellors, letters to Artaxerxes, and a stop-work order enforced by force and power. The work lay still until the second year of Darius, whose decree turned the tables: whoever altered it would be hanged on timber from his own house.
offense: The adversaries first offered to join the building, claiming to seek the same God. Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the chief fathers refused, declaring that they would build the house of the Lord according to Cyrus's command. The rejected offer was followed by open obstruction: the people of the land discouraged Judah, troubled the builders, and hired counselors to frustrate the work (Ezra 4:1-5). Ezra also records accusations against Jerusalem under later kings. Rehum and Shimshai represented the city as rebellious and warned that rebuilding would cost the king tribute and dominion. They obtained an order and enforced it by force and power (Ezra 4:11-23). Opposition clothed itself in concern for royal interests while working to weaken the returned people.
judgment: When the temple work resumed under Haggai and Zechariah, the elders continued while the inquiry went to Darius. The eye of their God was upon them (Ezra 5:5). A search recovered Cyrus's decree, and Darius ordered the work left alone and its expenses supplied from the royal tribute (Ezra 6:1-10). His decree threatened severe punishment against anyone who altered it. The account does not record that penalty being executed upon the earlier adversaries. It records their obstruction overcome: the elders built, the house was finished, and the children of the captivity dedicated it with joy. The authority invoked to hinder the work now required that it be supplied.

verses.text: Now when the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin heard that the children of the captivity builded the temple unto the Lord God of Israel;

Then they came to Zerubbabel, and to the chief of the fathers, and said unto them, Let us build with you: for we seek your God, as ye do; and we do sacrifice unto him since the days of Esar–haddon king of Assur, which brought us up hither.

But Zerubbabel, and Jeshua, and the rest of the chief of the fathers of Israel, said unto them, Ye have nothing to do with us to build an house unto our God; but we ourselves together will build unto the Lord God of Israel, as king Cyrus the king of Persia hath commanded us.
Then the people of the land weakened the hands of the people of Judah, and troubled them in building,
And hired counsellors against them, to frustrate their purpose, all the days of Cyrus king of Persia, even until the reign of Darius king of Persia.
This is the copy of the letter that they sent unto him, even unto Artaxerxes the king; Thy servants the men on this side the river, and at such a time.

Be it known unto the king, that the Jews which came up from thee to us are come unto Jerusalem, building the rebellious and the bad city, and have set up the walls thereof, and joined the foundations.
Be it known now unto the king, that, if this city be builded, and the walls set up again, then will they not pay toll, tribute, and custom, and so thou shalt endamage the revenue of the kings.
Now because we have maintenance from the king’s palace, and it was not meet for us to see the king’s dishonour, therefore have we sent and certified the king;

That search may be made in the book of the records of thy fathers: so shalt thou find in the book of the records, and know that this city is a rebellious city, and hurtful unto kings and provinces, and that they have moved sedition within the same of old time: for which cause was this city destroyed.
We certify the king that, if this city be builded again, and the walls thereof set up, by this means thou shalt have no portion on this side the river.

Now when the copy of king Artaxerxes’ letter was read before Rehum, and Shimshai the scribe, and their companions, they went up in haste to Jerusalem unto the Jews, and made them to cease by force and power.
Then ceased the work of the house of God which is at Jerusalem. So it ceased unto the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia.
Now therefore, Tatnai, governor beyond the river, Shethar–boznai, and your companions the Apharsachites, which are beyond the river, be ye far from thence:
Let the work of this house of God alone; let the governor of the Jews and the elders of the Jews build this house of God in his place.

Moreover I make a decree what ye shall do to the elders of these Jews for the building of this house of God: that of the king’s goods, even of the tribute beyond the river, forthwith expenses be given unto these men, that they be not hindered.

And that which they have need of, both young bullocks, and rams, and lambs, for the burnt offerings of the God of heaven, wheat, salt, wine, and oil, according to the appointment of the priests which are at Jerusalem, let it be given them day by day without fail:
That they may offer sacrifices of sweet savours unto the God of heaven, and pray for the life of the king, and of his sons.
Also I have made a decree, that whosoever shall alter this word, let timber be pulled down from his house, and being set up, let him be hanged thereon; and let his house be made a dunghill for this.

And the God that hath caused his name to dwell there destroy all kings and people, that shall put to their hand to alter and to destroy this house of God which is at Jerusalem. I Darius have made a decree; let it be done with speed.
Then Tatnai, governor on this side the river, Shethar–boznai, and their companions, according to that which Darius the king had sent, so they did speedily.

And the elders of the Jews builded, and they prospered through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah the son of Iddo. And they builded, and finished it, according to the commandment of the God of Israel, and according to the commandment of Cyrus, and Darius, and Artaxerxes king of Persia.
And this house was finished on the third day of the month Adar, which was in the sixth year of the reign of Darius the king.
But it came to pass, that when Sanballat heard that we builded the wall, he was wroth, and took great indignation, and mocked the Jews.

And he spake before his brethren and the army of Samaria, and said, What do these feeble Jews? will they fortify themselves? will they sacrifice? will they make an end in a day? will they revive the stones out of the heaps of the rubbish which are burned?
Now Tobiah the Ammonite was by him, and he said, Even that which they build, if a fox go up, he shall even break down their stone wall.
Hear, O our God; for we are despised: and turn their reproach upon their own head, and give them for a prey in the land of captivity:
And cover not their iniquity, and let not their sin be blotted out from before thee: for they have provoked thee to anger before the builders.
So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof: for the people had a mind to work.

entries.commentary: The adversaries of Judah and Benjamin hear of the building and come to Zerubbabel asking to build with them, claiming to seek the same God since the days of Esarhaddon king of Assur. These were peoples the king of Assyria had brought into the land, not true worshippers but taught only to appease the God of the land. -

Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the chief of the fathers refuse them: the strangers have nothing to do with building the house of the God of Israel. Israel would build to the Lord alone as Cyrus commanded. The forefathers understood that the work of the Most High is not shared with other nations.

The people of the land weaken the hands of Judah and trouble them in building. They hire counselors to frustrate the purpose all the days of Cyrus, even until the reign of Darius, a hindrance stretching across the kings in between.
In the reign of Ahasuerus and later Artaxerxes, the adversaries write accusations against the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem. The letter was written and interpreted in the Syrian tongue.

Rehum the chancellor and Shimshai the scribe write against Jerusalem, joined by the very nations the Assyrian king had set in the cities of Samaria. These are the same peoples named in [2 Kings 17](/bible/2-kings/17), brought over by the great and noble Asnappar, now bringing the accusation.

The letter warns the king that if Jerusalem is built the Jews will not pay toll, tribute, or custom, damaging the king's revenue. They call it a rebellious and hurtful city and urge the king to search the records to find cause to stop it.

The king answers that the records show Jerusalem made insurrection of old and had mighty kings who ruled beyond the river and received tribute. He commands the men to cease and the city not be built until another commandment is given from him.

When the letter is read, Rehum and Shimshai go up in haste to Jerusalem and make the Jews cease by force and power. The work of the house of God ceased until the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia. The same account, with a troop of horsemen halting the work, is told in 1 Esdras. -

Darius made search, and in the palace at Achmetha in the province of the Medes the roll was found recording the decree of Cyrus. The decree ordered the house rebuilt with strong foundations and set dimensions, the expenses given out of the king's house, and the gold and silver vessels restored to their place. Cyrus helped fund the rebuilding of the house of Israel.

Darius commanded Tatnai and his companions to leave the work alone and let the elders of the Jews build. He decreed that the cost be paid from the king's tribute beyond the river so the builders would not be hindered. Once a Persian decree was made it was upheld rather than vetoed. Even in Esther a decree against the Jews was not revoked but answered by a stronger decree in their favor. -

The king ordered daily provision of bullocks, rams, lambs, wheat, salt, wine, and oil so the priests could offer sacrifices without fail, and that they might pray for the life of the king and his sons. Whoever altered the decree was to be hanged on timber pulled from his own house, and his house made a dunghill. The God who caused his name to dwell there was called on to destroy any king or people who tried to destroy this house.

The elders prospered through the prophesying of Haggai and Zechariah and finished the house by the commandment of the Most High and of the Persian kings. The house was finished, and the children of the captivity kept the dedication with joy, offering a hundred bullocks, two hundred rams, four hundred lambs, and twelve he goats for a sin offering according to the number of the tribes of Israel. This was a great praise, and the Levites' hands were full doing the service. The priests were set in their divisions and the Levites in their courses as it is written in the book of Moses, every man having his ordered task. -

The children of the captivity kept the passover on the fourteenth day of the first month, for the priests and Levites were purified together and killed the passover for all the captivity. The passover can be kept in captivity with joyfulness and gladness of heart. Going back to the past shows how Israel is meant to operate, and these had the kingdom mindset to see the vision and finish the work.

When Sanballat hears that the wall is being built he is wroth, takes great indignation, and mocks the Jews. One of the heathen rulers rises up against the work, treating the rebuilding of Jerusalem as something to be scorned.

Before his brethren and the army of Samaria, Sanballat mocks the feeble Jews, asking if they will fortify themselves, sacrifice, finish in a day, and revive the burned stones out of the heaps of rubbish. He makes his mockery in front of his army, calling the people weak, the same way the heathen today mock the men who go out in one mind to do the work of the Most High.

Tobiah the Ammonite stands by him and says that even what they build, if a fox go up on it, would break down their stone wall. The enemy despises the work as flimsy, but the builders answer by praying that their reproach be turned upon their own head.

The wall is joined together to half its height, for the people had a mind to work. This is the pattern for Israel United in Christ today, a people with a mind to work who understand the condition of their people and the mission to rebuild their minds. -
Nehemiah answers the mockery with prayer, asking the Most High to turn the enemies' reproach upon their own heads.

When Sanballat, Tobiah, the Arabians, the Ammonites, and the Ashdodites hear that the walls are going up and the breaches are being stopped, they are very wroth. The breaches are the weaker places the enemies expected would fail. When they hear those gaps are fortified, their anger rises because their expectation of failure is broken.
They conspire together to come and fight against Jerusalem and to hinder the work. Their whole plan is to cause the work to cease and keep the city from being rebuilt. -
The builders make prayer to the Most High and set a watch against the enemies day and night.

Judah says the strength of the bearers of burdens is decayed, there is much rubbish, and they are not able to build the wall. Even among the workers the burden grows heavy and discouragement sets in as the enemy pressure mounts.

The adversaries say they will not be known or seen until they come into the midst and slay them and cause the work to cease. The enemies plot a surprise attack, aiming to kill the builders and stop the work entirely.

Nehemiah sets the people in the lower and higher places behind the wall after their families with their swords, spears, and bows. He arms the people by family and posts them at the exposed places, ready to defend the work.

Nehemiah tells the nobles, rulers, and people not to be afraid but to remember the Lord, who is great and terrible, and to fight for their brethren, sons, daughters, wives, and houses. The answer to fear is to remember the greatness of the Most High and to fight for the family and the people.

From that time half of the servants work while the other half hold the spears, shields, and bows, and the rulers stand behind all of Judah. The people labor and guard at the same time, knowing the enemies are plotting against the rebuilding.
Those who bear burdens work with one hand and hold a weapon with the other. Every builder keeps a weapon ready even while laying the wall, watchful against attack.

Every builder has his sword girded by his side as he builds, and the one who sounds the trumpet stays by Nehemiah. The trumpet becomes the signal to gather, keeping the scattered workers ready to unite at the point of attack.

Nehemiah tells the people that the work is great and large and they are separated far from one another along the wall. Because the builders are spread out, they need a plan to come together quickly if the enemy strikes.
Wherever they hear the sound of the trumpet, they are to resort there, for the Most High shall fight for them. The confidence of the builders rests on the truth that their God fights for them.
They labor in the work, half of them holding the spears from the rising of the morning until the stars appear. The people work from dawn to nightfall, giving the full day to the task.

Neither Nehemiah, his brethren, his servants, nor the men of the guard put off their clothes, saving only for washing. They are so serious about the work and so watchful that they stay dressed and ready at all times, of one mind to finish the wall, the same way the people are to be of one mind and one spirit today in the resurrection of the people.
